Cost assumptions

Costs start from the Sandia RM3 breakdown for 1, 10, 50 or 100 devices (SAND2014-9040), escalated from 2014 to 2026 dollars with the US consumer price index (×). Depth scales the mooring, the 50-year wave height scales structure and spares, shore distance adds export cable, and port distance adds vessel transit for installation and O&M. Changing a value re-ranks every site.

Data and validation

How to read this map in 60 seconds

Each dot is a candidate offshore site for a Sandia RM3 point absorber. The colour is the estimated cost of electricity from a 100-device array, in 2026 US dollars per kWh.

  1. Teal is cheapest, red is most expensive. The scale starts at the RM3 reference site (Humboldt, California). The open Pacific coast from California to Alaska stands out.
  2. The list on the left ranks the cheapest sites under the current filters: 40–100 m water depth and at most 60 km from shore. Click a row or a dot to open its site sheet.
  3. The site sheet shows energy per device (average and a conservative P90), the 50-year storm wave, distances to shore and port, the data source, and any protected-area or sea-ice flags.
  4. Change the assumptions under Cost assumptions (array size, vessel day rate, discount rate, cable cost). Every site is re-ranked instantly. The ranking barely moves under ±30% changes in any one cost.
  5. Check the confidence. US sites use a 200 m wave model checked against buoys. Canadian and Alaskan sites use an AI correction of global data, with a typical energy error of 5–16%. About the data gives the full validation.

RM3 is a public, unoptimised reference design. Compare sites with each other, not with grid prices.

Top 5 areas: one-page briefs

The best site in each area under the default screen: 40–100 m, at most 60 km from shore, confident sites, outside strict protected areas, 100 devices, default costs in 2026 US$. The cost range is the lowest and highest result when each cost assumption, and the AI energy estimate, is moved on its own.
